chapter: Complaints to Senator Eastland, FCC and WDSU
title: La Rocca on jazz club hypocrisy, integration and 'history by muddleheads'
summary: La Rocca says the jazz club honours Brown despite Sushan's 1949 letter, blames Stearns for starting integration, and says he wrote Senator Eastland.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Well, that'll show you what kind of people that the jazz club has and at the head of it. He wrote me in 1949 that I have proof that we were the original Dixieland jazz band. Now he's writing up on this guy that he is the original Dixieland jazz band. They give him a cup for his presence of being in the jazz club. What wonderful people they have in New Orleans. All they were doing was to start integration, what they call the mixing bowl. They had started that up north 22 years ago, 20 years ago, by Marshall Stein. Here's the first one started that business. It was brought to New Orleans. Yes. Yes. Many of my letters to different people. I've always mentioned the name is the history of jazz compiled by muggle heads, dope fiends, com-late prophets, self-aggrandizers, and many of these supposed to be historians filling their pocket up on poor, unfortunate musicians who never made anything at this music in the beginning. And now find a way that they can exploit these unfortunate men. And they're glad to get their name in the paper. So I listened to this propaganda. And I thought I was living in Russia, not the United States, the way some of this stuff was going on. My first idea was to try and interest someone into this kind of stuff was going on. I read in the paper where Senator Eastland was at the head of that committee. And he was from Mississippi. I wrote Senator Eastland, although he has never replied to me, but some action has been done in this matter. Do you want me to read it or you read this? I'll read it. All right. This is 1955.
